note: Transfer pool (SPEC_V2 §22): applying learned concepts to novel scenarios never used in lessons. Auto-scored; rationale shown after answering because practice feedback aids learning. Attempts record as stage 'transfer' and feed the mastery transfer component.

items.prompt: A city's rents rise 4 percent a year, compounding. A 1,000 euro rent after 2 years, in euros?
items.rationale: 1,000 x 1.04 x 1.04 = 1,081.60. Compounding applies to anything growing on its own base - rents, not just savings.

items.prompt: Your salary rises 3 percent while inflation runs 5 percent. In purchasing power you are:
items.rationale: Real change ≈ nominal minus inflation: 3 − 5 = −2 percent. The nominal raise is a real pay cut.

items.prompt: A company keeps 2 million euros idle in its account 'to stay safe' while similar firms earn 4 percent on short-term deposits. The true yearly cost of the choice is closest to:
items.rationale: Opportunity cost is the forgone alternative: 2,000,000 x 0.04 = 80,000 euros a year, unbilled but real.

items.prompt: A harvest failure halves the coffee crop while a health trend raises coffee demand. The price will:
items.rationale: Supply shifts left and demand shifts right - both movements push the price the same way: up.

items.prompt: Inflation runs hot and the central bank raises rates sharply. Which is the INTENDED first link of the chain?
options: borrowing becomes dearer, cooling spending and investment
items.answer: borrowing becomes dearer, cooling spending and investment
items.rationale: Policy rates transmit through borrowing costs to demand, and cooler demand slows price rises.

items.prompt: A US subscription costs 30 dollars monthly. The euro moves from 1.00 to 1.20 dollars per euro. The euro price falls by how many euros?
items.rationale: 30/1.00 = 30 euros before; 30/1.20 = 25 after. A stronger euro cut the bill by 5 euros.

items.prompt: An investor must sell a rarely-traded collectible-car fund quickly. Compared with selling a broad ETF, they should expect:
options: a worse price - illiquidity is paid for at exit
items.answer: a worse price - illiquidity is paid for at exit
items.rationale: Thin markets mean wide spreads and price impact: haste in an illiquid asset is expensive.

items.prompt: A bakery chain earns 600,000 euros on 12 million of revenue. A supermarket earns the same 600,000 on 60 million. The bakery's net margin is how many times the supermarket's?
items.rationale: 5 percent versus 1 percent - same profit, different business models. Margins, not raw profit, compare businesses.

items.prompt: News: 'government bond yields jumped today'. For existing holders of those bonds this means:
items.rationale: Yield and price are the same object read in opposite directions: yields up = prices down, immediately.

items.prompt: A pension fund holds bonds with duration 12. Yields fall 0.5 points. Approximate portfolio gain, in percent?
items.rationale: Δprice ≈ −duration x Δyield = −12 x (−0.5) = +6 percent. The lever works both ways.

items.prompt: Fund A: TER 0.15, tracking difference −0.35. Fund B: TER 0.25, tracking difference −0.22. Same index. The cheaper fund to actually hold was:
items.rationale: Tracking difference is the all-in realized cost; B delivered more of the index despite the higher sticker.

items.prompt: An engineer holds most savings in their own employer's stock 'because I know the company'. The overlooked risk is:
options: job and savings failing together - concentrated specific risk
items.answer: job and savings failing together - concentrated specific risk
items.rationale: Income and portfolio share one company's fate - the exact risk diversification deletes free of charge.

items.prompt: A fund returns +30 percent then −20 percent on 10,000 euros. End value, in euros?
items.rationale: 10,000 x 1.30 x 0.80 = 10,400 - a 2 percent compound rate despite the +5 average: volatility drag in action.

items.prompt: To cushion an equity portfolio against a panic, the most useful addition is an asset whose correlation to stocks:
options: is high in calm and crisis
does not matter if its return is high
items.rationale: Diversification's value in a panic comes from assets on different drivers - stock-stock correlations converge to 1 exactly then.

items.prompt: Safe rate 1 percent. A portfolio returns 7 percent at 12 volatility. Sharpe ratio, two decimals?
items.rationale: (7 − 1) / 12 = 0.50 of return per unit of risk - the comparable number, not the 7 alone.

items.prompt: A 60-year-old with adequate pensions and high calm during past crashes, versus a 30-year-old who sold everything in the last dip. Whose equity share should the QUESTIONNAIRE-perfect '100 minus age' rule most misjudge?
options: both - capacity and tolerance, not age formulas, set the share
items.answer: both - capacity and tolerance, not age formulas, set the share
items.rationale: The older investor's capacity and tolerance are high; the younger's tolerance is demonstrably low. Age proxies fail both directions.

items.prompt: Target 70/30. After a crash: stocks 49,000, bonds 31,000. How many euros of bonds must move into stocks?
items.rationale: Total 80,000; target stocks 56,000; buy 56,000 − 49,000 = 7,000 from bonds - the rule buys the crash on schedule.

items.prompt: A saver holds 8 funds: 3 world ETFs, 2 S&P 500 ETFs, 2 European ETFs, 1 bond fund. The portfolio is best described as:
options: roughly a two-fund portfolio with overlap and extra maintenance
items.answer: roughly a two-fund portfolio with overlap and extra maintenance
items.rationale: The seven equity funds correlate near +1 - breadth lives inside funds, not in their count.

items.prompt: A saver checks their portfolio daily and feels awful, though it is up over the year. The design flaw is:
options: daily sampling serves loss aversion a stream of felt losses
items.answer: daily sampling serves loss aversion a stream of felt losses
items.rationale: Markets zig-zag daily; each dip lands with doubled force. The same portfolio checked yearly feels like what it is: up.

items.prompt: An investor 'researches' a stock they already own by reading five bullish theses. The research mainly increased their:
items.rationale: Evidence collected to support a held view raises confidence, not correctness - the search for the case against was skipped.

items.prompt: A theme is everywhere: colleagues, feeds, record fund inflows, a tripled price. Historically, entering now most resembles:
options: buying near the top of a chase cycle
items.answer: buying near the top of a chase cycle
items.rationale: Saturated attention and peak inflows mark late-cycle herding - the crowd's comfort is maximal exactly where entry is worst.

items.prompt: Windfall of 10,000 euros. No reserve; a 4,000 euro credit balance at 16 percent; a funded portfolio. The order that follows the course's logic is:
options: all into the portfolio - highest expected return
reserve first, clear the 16 percent debt, remainder to the portfolio
clear the debt, rest to the portfolio, reserve later
items.answer: reserve first, clear the 16 percent debt, remainder to the portfolio
items.rationale: The reserve protects everything else from forced sales; the 16 percent repayment is a guaranteed return no market matches; investing takes what remains.

items.prompt: In a CTO you realize a 5,000 euro gain under the 31.4 percent flat tax. Euros kept after tax?
items.rationale: Tax 5,000 x 0.314 = 1,570; kept 3,430. Left unrealized, the full 5,000 would keep compounding.

items.prompt: A 28-year-old starts 200 euros monthly into a world-ETF strategy for retirement. The natural first wrapper is:
options: PEA - the five-year clock and income-tax exemption suit the horizon
items.answer: PEA - the five-year clock and income-tax exemption suit the horizon
items.rationale: Long-horizon equity saving fits the PEA's exemption; the clock argues for opening it now. CTO takes overflow; PER depends on bracket.
